You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.

According to the article, if you are unable to obtain a normal credit card, what are your alternatives?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	**Ten steps to rebuild your credit**
     2	
     3	There are many ways to rebuild credit, and the most effective options vary from person to person.
     4	Use this list of options as a starting point to make your own personalized plan to rebuild your
     5	credit.
     6	
     7	1. Get current with payments
     8	Before you do anything else to rebuild credit, make sure every account you have is current (not
     9	behind on payments). Accounts that are more than 30 days past due can do serious damage to your
    10	credit, and the later they get, the worse the damage will be.
    11	
    12	Plus, outstanding balances can mean late fees and interest fees get piled on top of your existing
    13	debt. The longer you're behind, the more expensive it'll be to catch up.
    14	
    15	If you're struggling to get current on your credit cards, make sure to contact your issuers. In most
    16	cases, a credit card issuer will work with you to establish a payment plan. After all, it's in the
    17	issuer's best interest for you to repay that debt.
    18	
    19	2. Pay down high balances
    20	One of the key factors used in credit scoring is called your credit utilization ratio. This is the
    21	ratio of how much credit card debt you have (amounts owed) versus your total available credit. For
    22	example, a credit card with a balance of $500 and a credit limit of $1,000 has a utilization ratio
    23	of of 50% ($500 / $1,000 = 0.5 x 10).
    24	
    25	High utilization (being close to your credit limits) is a warning sign to creditors that you may
    26	have taken on too much debt and could be living beyond your means. As a result, high utilization can
    27	hurt your credit score. One way to rebuild credit is to pay down those balances. The general rule of
    28	thumb is to keep your utilization below 30%. Try not to owe more than one-third of your credit
    29	limit; keeping your limit below 10% is ideal.
    30	
    31	Building a budget that prioritizes debt repayment is often the best method for paying down high
    32	balances. See below for more information on budgets, or our guide to paying off debt for our top
    33	tips.
    34	
    35	If you're already living on a tight budget, a debt consolidation loan may be a good way to pay down
    36	credit cards and boost your credit score. Opening a debt consolidation loan can bring down your
    37	score in the short term, but can benefit your score in the long term. If changing your budget isn't
    38	an option, it's worth investigating whether a debt consolidation loan is right for you.
    39	
    40	3. Pay on time, every time
    41	Every time you make a credit card payment and the issuer reports your payment to the credit bureaus,
    42	you are contributing to your payment history. Your payment history is the most important part of
    43	your credit score.
    44	
    45	No plan to rebuild credit will work if you aren't making payments on time. Make at least your
    46	minimum required payment by the due date every single month. (Ideally, pay off your entire balance
    47	every month to avoid credit card interest fees.)
    48	
    49	4. Activate automatic payments
    50	If you're having trouble remembering due dates, you can let the credit card company take care of it
    51	for you. Most banks and issuers will allow you to set up automatic payments. You can choose the
    52	amount you want to pay -- make sure it's at least your minimum payment -- as well as when you want
    53	the payments to process.
    54	
    55	If you don't have automatic payments set to cover your entire monthly bill, be sure to follow up
    56	with additional payments to pay your full balance.
    57	
    58	5. Keep balances low
    59	As mentioned, your utilization rate has a lot of influence on your credit score. Once you've paid
    60	down your outstanding balances, make sure to keep them low.
    61	
    62	You'll struggle to rebuild credit if you keep running up your credit card balances after paying them
    63	down. People with excellent credit tend to have utilization rates below 10%.
    64	
    65	6. Open a secured credit card
    66	The only surefire way to rebuild credit is to have a recent positive payment history. Of course, if
    67	your credit is heavily damaged, you may have trouble qualifying for a credit card with which to
    68	build that payment history. This is where a secured credit card can help.
    69	
    70	Secured credit cards can be pretty easy to get, even if your credit is damaged. That's because
    71	secured cards rely on a cash security deposit to minimize risk to the issuer. If you pay off your
    72	balance in full, you'll get the security deposit back when you close your account. Some issuers will
    73	even automatically upgrade you to an unsecured account and return your deposit.
    74	
    75	7. Become an authorized user on someone else's card
    76	Another way to rebuild credit is to be added as an authorized user on another person's card (such as
    77	a trusted family member). When you become an authorized user on someone else's credit card, you
    78	receive your own credit card with your name. But the credit account is still the responsibility of
    79	the primary account holder. The card company typically reports the credit card account to the credit
    80	bureaus for both the primary account holder and the authorized user.
    81	
    82	As long as the account is in good standing, being added as an authorized user can help raise your
    83	credit score.
    84	
    85	Being an authorized user isn't without risks, however. For example, if the cardholder or the
    86	authorized user runs up a high balance, both users could see credit score damage. Only tie your
    87	credit score to individuals you trust.
    88	
    89	8. Build a budget -- and stick to it
    90	Any plan to rebuild credit score damage is sure to fail if you don't address the root of the
    91	problem. In many cases, the root cause boils down to the lack of a budget -- and yes, that means a
    92	realistic budget, not an idealized one. If your budget doesn't reflect your actual lifestyle,
    93	spending, and debts, it'll be useless.
    94	
    95	A good budget can help you repay debts and keep from overextending yourself in the future.
    96	
    97	RELATED: Best Budgeting Apps
    98	
    99	9. Keep an eye on your credit reports and scores
   100	As you work to rebuild credit, be sure to check up on your credit reports and scores regularly. Many
   101	credit card issuers offer free monthly credit scores, especially on credit-building products. You
   102	can also get free copies of your credit reports from each of the three bureaus once a year through
   103	AnnualCreditReport.com.
   104	
   105	If you find any errors on your reports, be sure to dispute them quickly with the credit bureaus.
   106	
   107	10. Give it time
   108	Like it or not, sometimes time is the only way to rebuild credit. Those delinquent payments and
   109	defaulted accounts aren't going anywhere fast.
   110	
   111	It can take years of building a positive payment history to recover from big mistakes -- especially
   112	when those mistakes can sit on your reports for up to seven years. If you're doing everything right
   113	to rebuild your credit, but you're not seeing much movement in your credit scores: be patient. Time
   114	-- and keeping on top of your payments -- heals most credit wounds.
   115	
   116	How long will it take to rebuild my credit?
   117	Every credit profile is unique. As a result, the best strategy for rebuilding credit will depend on
   118	your credit history and the reasons for your credit problems. In other words, the answer to the
   119	question of "How long does it take to rebuild credit?" is: It depends.

121	A low credit score caused by high credit card balances can be the quickest thing to fix (assuming
   122	you have the funds to pay them off). Paying down high balances can help you rebuild credit in 30
   123	days or less.
   124	
   125	On the other hand, if you need to rebuild credit due to late payments or a defaulted account, you're
   126	probably going to need longer. It will take at least six to 12 months to rebuild credit scores to an
   127	acceptable level -- and several years for the negative items to disappear altogether.
   128	
   129	In fact, negative items can linger on your credit reports for up to 10 years in certain cases
   130	(primarily bankruptcy), with most negative items having a shelf life of seven years. On the bright
   131	side, negative items impact your credit scores less as they age, particularly when you've been
   132	building a positive payment history in the meantime.
   133	
   134	How can I raise my credit score by 100 points?
   135	If you have very high credit utilization -- meaning you're close to your credit limits -- paying
   136	down your balances could provide a large credit score boost. Credit scores damaged by credit report
   137	errors can also jump quite a bit when those errors are removed.
   138	
   139	Outside of these situations, however, you'll typically need to rebuild credit over many months to
   140	see a gain of 100 points or more. There is no guaranteed way to raise your credit score by a
   141	specific amount -- and 100 points is a lot to expect. For example, a 100-point jump from 570 to 670
   142	moves you from bad credit into fair credit.
   143	
   144	What type of credit cards work for rebuilding credit?
   145	The best credit cards to rebuild credit have minimal costs and report your payments to the credit
   146	bureaus each month. This means cards with affordable annual fees -- or, even better, credit cards
   147	with no annual fees -- and the option to make automatic payments.
   148	
   149	Wondering where to start? A number of credit cards for fair or average credit won't charge a fee. If
   150	you can't qualify for an unsecured card without an annual fee, consider a secured credit card
   151	instead.
   152	
   153	Secured cards differ from traditional cards in one key way: the deposit. Secured credit cards
   154	require an upfront cash deposit to open and maintain. This makes them safer for the issuer. Even if
   155	you have significant credit damage, you can likely find an issuer willing to offer you a secured
   156	credit card.
   157	
   158	Banks where you already have a good reputation and your local credit union are often the best places
   159	to find a secured card. Look for one that might allow you to graduate easily to an unsecured card
   160	(and avoid annual fees, if possible).

According to `doc.txt`, if you can't qualify for a regular (unsecured) credit card, the article offers two alternatives:

1. **Open a secured credit card.** The article says secured cards "can be pretty easy to get, even if your credit is damaged," because they rely on a cash security deposit to minimize risk to the issuer. If you pay off your balance in full, you get the security deposit back when you close the account, and some issuers will even automatically upgrade you to an unsecured account and return your deposit. The article also notes that banks where you already have a good reputation and your local credit union are often the best places to find a secured card, and to look for one that might allow you to graduate easily to an unsecured card (and avoid annual fees, if possible).

2. **Become an authorized user on someone else's card** (such as a trusted family member). You receive your own credit card with your name on it, but the account remains the responsibility of the primary account holder, and the card company typically reports the account to the credit bureaus for both the primary holder and the authorized user. As long as the account is in good standing, this can help raise your credit score. The article cautions that this isn't without risks: if the cardholder or the authorized user runs up a high balance, both users could see credit score damage, so you should only tie your credit score to individuals you trust.
